places.now: King's Cross area; the name survives only in Battle Bridge Road and Battle Bridge Place behind the station
places.reason: Battle Bridge was the old name of the King's Cross district on the Fleet river crossing, renamed King's Cross in the 1830s; the gazetteer guess lies in the right area but the district is broader.

places.now: fictional; Canterbury city centre (King's School and St Dunstan's streets are often suggested)
places.reason: Dr Strong's school is fictional and given no exact site, so the coordinates are only a Canterbury city-centre guess.

places.now: Gerrard Street, the centre of London's Chinatown
places.reason: A well-documented street in Soho running east-west north of Leicester Square, and unchanged in line since the 18th century.

places.now: Hampton Court Palace, a historic royal palace and museum
places.reason: A famous, well-documented Tudor palace on the Thames, still standing where it was in Dickens's time.

places.now: Inner Temple, one of the four Inns of Court, between Fleet Street and the Embankment
places.reason: One of the Inns of Court off Fleet Street; the gazetteer guess is correct, though much was rebuilt after WWII bombing.

places.now: Wapping; the docks were closed in 1969 and mostly filled in, leaving Tobacco Dock, warehouses and Hermitage basins
places.reason: The London Docks occupied a large area of Wapping north of Wapping High Street, so this is a central point and the gazetteer's church match is only nearby.

places.now: Central Criminal Court (Old Bailey), on the site of Newgate Prison
places.reason: The Old Bailey sessions house stood beside Newgate Prison; the present building opened in 1907 on the Newgate site, and the gazetteer guess is right.

places.now: Sahara Desert, North Africa
places.reason: A real region whose centre is placed here, though Dickens uses it figuratively, so only a regional point is meaningful.

places.now: Adelphi area between the Strand and the Thames; the Adam terraces were demolished in the 1930s and replaced by the Art Deco Adelphi building on John Adam Street
places.reason: The Adam brothers' riverside development off the Strand, with the arches beneath it, was the Adelphi of Dickens's day; the gazetteer's theatre match is nearby on the Strand.

places.now: Alps, mountain range in France, Switzerland, Italy and Austria
places.reason: A mountain range with no single point; the coordinate is a central Swiss Alps point, and the gazetteer match (a Grenoble company) is wrong.

places.now: Balls Pond Road area, between Islington, Dalston and De Beauvoir; the pond is long gone
places.reason: The name belonged to a suburban district on the Kingsland-Essex Road route and survives in Balls Pond Road, so this is an approximate point along it.

places.now: Brentford, in the London Borough of Hounslow
places.reason: Brentford was a Middlesex town on the Thames and the Brent; the gazetteer's Middlesex Court is just an arbitrary nearby building, so the town centre is the better fix.

places.now: Lincoln's Inn Old Hall still stands; the court moved to the Royal Courts of Justice in the Strand in 1882
places.reason: In the 1830s-60s Chancery sat at Lincoln's Inn Old Hall in term and at Westminster Hall at other times; Dickens's scene is usually located at Lincoln's Inn.

places.now: fictional; the area is around Leicester Square
places.reason: Mr George's gallery is fictional, and Bleak House places it in a back street near Leicester Square, so this is a rough guess.

places.now: Great St Bernard Pass, on the Swiss-Italian border, with the hospice and a road tunnel below
places.reason: A famous alpine pass with a hospice at the summit; the coordinates are those of the pass summit.

places.now: fictional; the nearby Cursitor Street (Cook's Court in the novel) is around here
places.reason: Krook's shop is fictional, set in a court by Chancery Lane (Cook's Court is usually identified with Cursitor Street), so the coordinates are an educated guess.

places.now: former county of Middlesex, now mostly in Greater London (north-west of the Thames) and partly Surrey
places.reason: A historic county that included the northern half of the London area; the point is a rough centroid, and the gazetteer's Supreme Court match is just the old Middlesex Guildhall building.

places.now: fictional pub; the Cursitor Street area near Chancery Lane is the likely setting
places.reason: The Sol's Arms is a fictional pub in Cook's Court near Chancery Lane, probably based on a real inn there, so the point is a guess.

places.now: fictional; the area was cleared for the London & Birmingham Railway near Camden and Euston
places.reason: Staggs's Gardens is fictional, an amalgam of the Camden Town district destroyed by the railway cutting near Euston, so this point is approximate.

places.now: Imperial War Museum London, in the former Bethlem building in Lambeth Road
places.reason: Bethlem Hospital occupied the Lambeth Road site in St George's Fields from 1815 to 1930, so the gazetteer guess is correct for Dickens's day.

places.now: Clifford's Inn site, with surviving gatehouse and flats around Clifford's Inn Passage off Fleet Street
places.reason: A former Inn of Chancery north of Fleet Street between Chancery Lane and Fetter Lane, sold in 1903 and partly demolished; the gazetteer guess is correct.

places.now: A2 (Old Kent Road and Watling Street) from London to Dover
places.reason: The Dover Road is a long route, here marked at its London start on the Old Kent Road, and its scenes lie along the whole of it.

places.now: The Downs, a sheltered anchorage in the North Sea between Deal and the Goodwin Sands
places.reason: A well-known roadstead off the Kent coast; the coordinate is its approximate centre.

places.now: Kingston upon Thames, a town in south-west London
places.reason: A well-known Surrey market town on the Thames, and the gazetteer's New Malden business is the wrong place.

places.now: Demolished; only a surviving wall remains in Angel Place beside Southwark library, off Borough High Street
places.reason: The Marshalsea debtors' prison stood on the east side of Borough High Street and was closed in 1842; the lodge was the entrance, and the exact spot is approximate.
